Human teams excel at dynamically restructuring both task assignments and
team composition in response to emerging challenges, proactively recruiting
or releasing members as needed. This capacity for autonomous adaptation is a
cornerstone of effective teamwork, yet remains difﬁcult to achieve in het-
erogeneous multi-robot systems, which typically operate under ﬁxed team
conﬁgurations or adapt only responsively to external disruptions. In this work,
we present a systematic investigation of the Proactive Collaboration paradigm
for robot teams, where the working team autonomously recruits or releases
members as tasks evolve. We implement this paradigm by equipping robots
with the developed Autonomous Interaction framework, which utilizes need-
driven multi-round communication to facilitate discussions over task pro-
gress, negotiated task allocation, and dynamic team resizing. Through real-
world and simulated experiments, we demonstrate that our framework
effectively realizes the Proactive Collaboration. By resolving capability gaps via
anticipatory planning and minimizing action redundancy, it yields consistent
and measurable gains in team efﬁciency and robustness. Our ﬁndings suggest
that enabling individual-level initiative may offer a promising pathway toward
more adaptive and cohesive collective behavior in multi-robot systems.
Real-world scenarios, ranging from indoor services to disaster
response and planetary exploration, increasingly require multi-robot
teams to address tasks too complex for individual agents1,2. While
heterogeneous robot teams provide diverse capabilities to handle
environmental variability3–7, the challenge lies in the unpredictable
evolution of task demands during execution. Given this unpredict-
ability, it is unrealistic to determine the optimal multi-robot team
composition in advance or to deploy an entire large team simulta-
neously. Instead, the adaptability of the team is critically enhanced by
allowing agents to be added or removed as needed, enabling them to
autonomously redistribute tasks and solicit collaboration under
uncertainty. Therefore, it is necessary for the team to support on-
demand team reconﬁguration during task execution, a paradigm that
imposes exceptionally high demands on the robots’ collaboration and
communication strategies8.
For robot teams united by a shared goal, collaboration paradigms
are generally categorized based on whether the team composition
evolves during task execution: Fixed and Dynamic paradigms1,9. The
former operates with a pre-determined membership, while the latter
allows the composition to be reshaped by adding or removing team
members. Fixed Collaboration is widely utilized due to its simple
design and ease of deployment, often initiated by manual determina-
tion or algorithmic optimization10–13. However, this rigid structure
inherently results in the team lacking the resilience necessary to adapt
to dynamic environmental changes or unexpected failures. Con-
versely, Dynamic Collaboration signiﬁcantly enhances the adaptability

of the robot team and holds broad potential for resolving complex,
evolving tasks. Despite these advantages, realizing such dynamic col-
laboration faces challenges regarding the underlying mechanisms of
adaptation. Speciﬁcally, identifying the exact timing and precise
requirements for restructuring remains a critical bottleneck that has
signiﬁcantly hindered its widespread application14.
To elucidate how existing systems tackle this bottleneck, we
analyze the triggers driving team composition changes, categorizing
dynamic collaboration into two distinct paradigms: Responsive Col-
laboration and Proactive Collaboration (Fig. 1). As contrasted against
the rigid failure of Fixed Collaboration, the key distinction between
these two dynamic paradigms lies in whether the team reconﬁguration
is driven by passive external intervention or active internal foresight.
The Responsive Collaboration paradigm addresses scenarios where
team composition changes are imposed by external events rather than
the working team’s initiative, such as robot failures or the arrival of new
agents. This category encompasses research domains such as ad hoc
teamwork15–19 and dynamic team formation20,21, which typically rely on
mechanisms like market-based auctions20, opportunistic encounters21, or
open-team policy learning18,22. However, external entities or algorithms
often lack full situational awareness of the working team’s speciﬁc con-
text, preventing timely and precise interventions. Simultaneously, the
working team operates without anticipating these composition changes.
Consequently, task reallocation occurs only after the team membership
has been externally altered. This passive adaptation limits the team’s
ability to effectively resolve capability gaps, leading to delayed, mis-
aligned, and inefﬁcient execution trajectories.
In contrast, human teams typically exhibit the Proactive Colla-
boration paradigm, characterized by the team’s autonomous decision
to dynamically reshape its composition as the task evolves. Rooted in
cognitive empathy and shared situational awareness, experts in high-
stakes domains such as emergency medicine and disaster response
routinely form temporary coalitions to address urgent challenges23–25.
In these scenarios, teams do not wait for external dispatchers to
identify needs (Responsive). Instead, they actively call for specialists
(e.g., Rapid Response Teams) to bridge capability gaps, thereby miti-
gating delays and information asymmetry23,26–28. Recognizing that
autonomous adaptation rooted in cognitive empathy is a key driver of
collective intelligence29–31, we aim to realize this mechanism in robotic
systems. To support such autonomy, individual agents must possess
robust capabilities in situated perception, semantic reasoning, and
autonomous arbitration32. Moving beyond existing help-seeking fra-
meworks that rely on human-in-the-loop assistance33–37, we claim that
Proactive Collaboration requires agents to autonomously determine
when to seek help, whom to ask, and what to communicate. By mas-
tering these dimensions, the team can anticipate capability gaps and
proactively recruit specialists or release redundant members, ensuring
an aligned and efﬁcient execution ﬂow.
However, realizing such a mechanism remains an open problem
due to three complexities. First, determining when to initiate interac-
tion is critical, requiring agents to semantically identify help-seeking
needs and the team to optimize the timing for reconﬁguration. Sec-
ond, deciding whom to target involves selecting appropriate helpers
from internal members or external candidates. This process compli-
cates task planning, as the system must dynamically determine whe-
ther to recruit new members or release redundant ones to align with
varying capabilities. Finally, establishing what to communicate neces-
sitates an effective mechanism to synchronize these decisions, ensur-
ing smooth collaboration throughout the process.
To overcome these complexities, we identify Foundation Models as
the ideal cognitive foundation, leveraging their emerging capabilities in
robotic reasoning, ranging from embodied planning38,39 and task
allocation40–45 to code generation46–49, as well as in the social simulation
of complex collaborative dynamics50,51. Building on this, we propose the
Autonomous Interaction framework that integrates individual robot
intelligence with a multi-robot coordination mechanism. Each robot
follows a two-layer architecture: an Embodiment Layer that closes the
perception, action, and reﬂection loop for situated reasoning and
embodied taskexecution52,53, anda Communicative Reasoning Layer that
converts local states and reﬂections into structured, goal-directed mes-
sages. On top of this per-robot capability, the team coordination is
organized by Autonomous Need-Driven Communication, which triggers
multi-round dialogs when necessary. This allows robots to deliberate
over task progress, negotiate assignments, and dynamically recruit or
release teammates to match the evolving requirements.
In summary, this work establishes an Autonomous Interaction
framework that realizes Proactive Collaboration by enabling hetero-
geneous robot teams to anticipate capability gaps and restructure
their composition. We further show that Large Language Models are
capable of leveraging individual initiative to augment team perfor-
mance. Finally, we validate the performance across both real-world
experiments and extensive simulations, supported by our introduction
of DynaTeamTHOR, a benchmark designed for the systematic eva-
luation of dynamic collaboration.

formulation and experimental design, which establishes the criteria for
evaluating ﬁxed, responsive, and proactive team collaboration para-
digms (Sec. 2.1). Next, we introduce the Autonomous Interaction fra-
mework that integrates individual robot intelligence with a multi-robot
coordination mechanism to support efﬁcient teamwork (Sec. 2.2).
Building on this architecture, we validate the feasibility and effective-
ness of the Proactive Collaboration paradigm through real-world
experiments, demonstrating the system’s adaptability to physical
constraints and changing task requirements (Sec. 2.3). To further
substantiate the algorithmic effectiveness of our method, we employ
the scalable DynaTeamTHOR simulation benchmark to demonstrate
its advantages over baselines under consistent paradigm settings (Sec.
2.3). Finally, we conduct a ﬁne-grained failure analysis to elucidate the
mechanisms underlying the observed performance gains and failure
mode shifts (Sec. 2.5).
Experimental setup
Embodied Tidying-up Task. We evaluate multi-robot collaboration on
an embodied tidying-up task54,55. In this setup, a heterogeneous team
acts within an indoor environment to explore, identify misplaced
objects, infer their correctgoal locations, and physically relocate them.
Crucially, the task may necessitate coordinated interaction (e.g.,
clearing obstacles for a teammate) whenever the requirements exceed
individual capabilities. Representative real-world task instances are
shown in Fig. 2. Overall, this process demands both high-level semantic
reasoning and precise team coordination.
Team Model. To implement collaboration under practical con-
straints, we introduce a team model that separates agents inside the
active operation (the working team) from available resources outside
the workspace (the robot pool). This structured boundary reﬂects the
resource management required in broader real-world applications,
such as buffering standby units in last-mile logistics or staging backup
units in warehouse scenarios, as further discussed in Sec. 3. Based on
this boundary control, we instantiate three distinct experimental
conditions:
• Fixed paradigm (Controlled Baseline): The boundary is closed.
The team operates with a ﬁxed membership determined at initi-
alization, prohibiting entry or exit regardless of task demands.
• Responsive paradigm (Baseline): The boundary is semi-permeable
but passive. Agents are dispatched from the pool based on the
assessment of an external monitoring dispatcher, which deter-
mines when intervention is necessary.
• Proactive paradigm (Ours): The boundary is permeable and team-
controlled. The working team autonomously manages recruit-
ment or release of members based on evolving task requirements
and internal team assessments.
Experimental Design. Our evaluation combines real-world and
simulation studies to provide complementary evidence.
In real-world experiments, to validate paradigm feasibility, we
deployed the proposed Autonomous Interaction framework as the
uniform underlying driver for all three paradigm variants (Fixed,
Responsive, and Proactive). This controlled setting serves to demon-
strate how the Proactive paradigm unlocks ﬂexibility and efﬁciency by
dynamically adjusting team composition.
Complementing this, simulation experiments focus on verifying
algorithmic superiority. Here, we hold the paradigm settings constant
and benchmark the proposed Autonomous Interaction against repre-
sentative baseline methods. Under matched task distributions, we seek
to validate that our framework consistently achieves higher efﬁciency
and decision quality. Additionally, this comparative analysis investi-
gates the hypothesis that the efﬁciency gains of the Proactive para-
digm are realized only through a capable interaction mechanism.
Metrics Overview. We focus our evaluation on a uniﬁed set of
primary metrics characterizing task success and execution efﬁciency.
Speciﬁcally, we report Success Rate (SR: a binary indicator of whether
an episode fully succeeds) and Partial Success Rate (PS: the fraction of
objects correctly placed, simulation only). To measure efﬁciency, we
use Temporal Steps (TS: the number of environment steps until ter-
mination) and Total Action Steps (AS: the total number of executed
action steps summed across all robots, simulation only). For full deﬁ-
nitions and auxiliary metrics, please refer to Sec. 4.3.
Autonomous interaction framework
As illustrated in Fig. 3, the proposed Autonomous Interaction frame-
work integrates individual robot intelligence with a multi-robot coor-
dination mechanism. This hierarchical design bridges high-level
semantic reasoning with low-level execution, providing the necessary
infrastructure for dynamic role assignment and team reconﬁguration
(details in Sec. 4).
Individual robot architecture. At the individual level, each robot
integrates a dual-layer architecture comprising an Embodiment Layer
for physical interaction and a Communicative Reasoning Layer for
high-level coordination. (details in Sec. 4.1)
The Embodiment Layer handles the fundamental embodiment cycle:
the Visual Semantic Perception module transforms sensory data into
structured semantic text (e.g., “pillow on ﬂoor, between bed and wall") to
facilitate downstream reasoning. Based on this context, the Action Deci-
sion module formulates immediate actions executed by the Action
Execution module. Crucially, to support proactive need identiﬁcation, the
State Assessment module acts as a continuous self-monitor. It triggers a
request for help under two speciﬁc conditions: (i) when execution fails
(e.g., physical inability), or (ii) when perception identiﬁes a demand
exceeding current capabilities (e.g., a “heavy" attribute).
The bridge between individual action and collective coordination
is the Communicative Reasoning layer. This layer comprises two dis-
tinct modules designed to handle information ﬂow at different stages
of the interaction.
• Purposeful Expression: This module facilitates in-communication
message generation by ensuring that every utterance is strategi-
cally aligned with the robot’s current objectives. To ensure
coherent and goal-oriented exchange, this module decouples
message generation into a two-stage process. During an active
dialog, the Thinking Stage ﬁrst synthesizes the Incoming Message
and internal Reﬂection to establish a clear communicative
Purpose. Based on this intent, the Speaking Stage then formulates
the Outgoing Message. This explicit abstraction prevents redun-
dant or off-topic utterances, ensuring that communication
remains an efﬁcient tool for problem-solving rather than an end
in itself.
• Task Summary: This module performs the post-communication
task update by anchoring collective consensus into the robot’s
individual execution pipeline. Once the Autonomous Need-Driven
Communication protocol signals the end of a negotiation, this
module analyzes the entire Message History to extract actionable
consensus. It distillates the multi-robot agreement into a localized
task update, effectively translating collective decisions into the
robot’s next individual Task. By updating the local plan of each
participant, this module ensures synchronized role changes and
goal alignment across the heterogeneous team without the need
for a central orchestrator.
Autonomous need-driven communication. At the collective
level, the framework utilizes Autonomous Need-Driven Communica-
tion to manage task allocation and member recruitment. This protocol

Once the Autonomous Need-Driven Communication concludes
that a consensus has been achieved, the Task Summary module per-
forms the post-communication task update by conducting a ﬁnal
consolidation of the entire Message History. It distills the negotiated
agreements into updated local plans for all involved agents, ensuring
synchronized role transitions and seamless task handovers across the
heterogeneous team without a central controller.
Real-world validation
To validate the feasibility of the Proactive Collaboration paradigm in a
physical setting, we deployed a heterogeneous team in an ofﬁce
environment comprising four interconnected rooms with both spatial
and functional complexity.
Platform and environment. We utilized a pool of ﬁve hetero-
geneous robots positioned outside the main workspace to represent
available resources, as shown in Fig. 4a–f. The speciﬁc platforms inclu-
ded: (a) Car(AgileXLIMO) and(e)Go2(Unitree Go2)forrapidperception
and navigation; (b) AlienGo (Unitree AlienGo) for locomotion and
manipulation; (c) Stretch (Hello Robot Stretch) for complex physical
interaction and high-reach manipulation; and (d) Cleaner (iRobot Cre-
ate3) for surface cleaning. These platforms provide complementary
mobility and interaction capabilities. To join the working team, robots
from the pool must physically enter the active workspace through a
designated entrance, which restricts local perception to deployed robots
and formally marks their state transition from an external resource to an
active team member. Details of the robotic platforms and sensor con-
ﬁgurations are provided in Supplementary Sec. 1.1.1.
Evaluation protocol. We evaluated the three paradigms (Fixed,
Responsive, and Proactive) across a total of 60 episodes, following a
full factorial design of 3 paradigms × 10 scenarios × 2 initial team
conﬁgurations. To test adaptability, we designed ten cluttered multi-
room scenarios varying in difﬁculty: 4 instances requiring basic coor-
dination and 6 instances demanding complex interaction (e.g., cart
pulling) or auxiliary cleaning.
To emulate the scenario of dispatching a robot team into a room
with unknown task requirements, we initialized the teams without
prior knowledge of the speciﬁc obstacles or messes they would
encounter. Consequently, these initial teams may possess varying
degrees of capability gaps relative to the actual demand. We modeled
this by initiating tasks with two distinct conﬁgurations: a basic
conﬁguration capable of standard tasks but vulnerable to high-load
demands, and an intermediate conﬁguration with improved versatility
but remaining incomplete for comprehensive scenarios. This design
speciﬁcally stresses the system’s ability to recognize capability gaps
and adjust team composition dynamically under unknown task
distributions.
End-to-end performance. As shown in Fig. 4g, the choice of
collaboration paradigm signiﬁcantly impacts the team’s overall suc-
cess and efﬁciency. The Fixed paradigm struggled with capability gaps,
achieving the lowest Success Rate (SR) of 0.45 and the highest average
completion time of 931 seconds. The Responsive Paradigm provided a
slight improvement (SR 0.55, 894s) by allowing external help, but its
performance remained capped by both the dispatch delay and the
post-arrival integration latency. In contrast, the Proactive Paradigm
achieved a dominant SR of 0.90 with the lowest average time of 735s.
This substantial leap validates that enabling the team to autonomously
anticipate needs and recruit members signiﬁcantly reduces failure
rates and execution time.
Coordination quality and team dynamics. To decouple coor-
dination stability from resource availability, we analyze the Condi-
tional Success Rate (Fig. 4h). This metric calculates the success rate
exclusively for the subset of episodes where a capable team was suc-
cessfully formed, thereby isolating the impact of the collaboration
strategy on execution consistency:
• Inherent Framework Competence (Fixed): For the Fixed para-
digm, we calculate this metric over the subset of episodes where
the initial team conﬁguration was already theoretically sufﬁcient.
The high score of 0.82 serves as a controlled baseline, demon-
strating that our underlying Autonomous Interaction framework
effectively organizes the team when resources are present and
secured from the start.
• Passive Integration Cost (Responsive): In the Responsive para-
digm, we isolate the speciﬁc episodes where external intervention
successfully provided the necessary agents. Despite eventually
acquiring the required resources, the paradigm shows a sig-
niﬁcant drop in conditional success to 0.61. This indicates that the
passive introduction of new members often creates coordination
misalignment rather than cohesion. Such sudden additions dis-
rupt the existing collaboration, often causing the task to fail even
when the team gains the necessary capabilities.

• Proactive Efﬁciency Gain (Proactive): For the Proactive paradigm,
we evaluate episodes where the working team successfully iden-
tiﬁed and recruited the required members. This approach
achieves the highest conditional success rate of 0.90, surpassing
even the stable Fixed baseline. This suggests that proactive
recruitment acts as more than just a resource buffer. By seeking
help at the appropriate moment, the team integrates new mem-
bers seamlessly before conﬂicts escalate, turning potential coor-
dination friction into an efﬁciency gain.
Collectively, these ﬁndings demonstrate that the anticipatory planning
of reconﬁguration is as critical as the resources themselves: whereas
passive intervention incurs a coordination penalty, proactive antici-
pation enables the team to effectively integrate new members to
enhance, rather than merely repair, the workﬂow.
Representative episode. The efﬁciency of the Proactive paradigm
stems from its ability to bridge capability gaps in real-time. As illustrated
in Fig. 5 (and representative tasks in Fig. 2), when an initial team
encounters a “trapped bottle" requiring heavy manipulation, the system
identiﬁes the deﬁciency and autonomously recruits Stretch from the
robot pool. Once Stretch clears the obstacle (the cart), it allows the
original team to proceed. Furthermore, the system dynamically releases
robots (e.g., Car and Go2) once their tasks are complete, optimizing team
size without human intervention. A full video demonstration of this task
episode is available in Supplementary Video 2.
Mechanisms of Adaptability. The signiﬁcant performance
advantage of the Proactive paradigm (90% SR vs. 55% in Responsive)
stems from two primary mechanisms. First, the team autonomously
recruits members during execution, ensuring the group composition
aligns with task demands and eliminating the signiﬁcant waiting
latency caused by late external intervention. Second, and crucially, the
Proactive paradigm incorporates anticipatory planning to coordinate
the team’s state for the speciﬁc helper’s arrival. As visualized in Fig. 6,
the Responsive paradigm suffers from a prolonged “misaligned action"
phase (Integration Latency) even after the required robot eventually
arrives. In contrast, the Proactive paradigm orchestrates the recruit-
ment process, enabling direct coordination where the helper inte-
grates into the workﬂow immediately.

Controlled experiments in simulation
Simulation Benchmark: DynaTeamTHOR. To enable statistically
grounded comparisons for our proposed Autonomous Interaction
framework, we introduce DynaTeamTHOR, which extends the cap-
abilities of the AI2-THOR series56,57. The environment features realistic
3D indoor scenes rich in semantic diversity, ranging from living areas
to kitchens, each populated with interactive objects and varied furni-
ture layouts. It operationalizes our team model through two key fea-
tures: (i) A Coordinated Interaction Mechanism that mandates
synchronized joint actions to trigger speciﬁc state changes (e.g., dis-
placing heavy furniture). This explicitly enables “Trapped Object"
scenarios, where target items are occluded by obstacles that require
collaborative displacement to access. And (ii) A Dynamic Robot Pool
Interface that enables multiple robots to operate simultaneously
within the same multi-room workspace, allowing real-time agent
instantiation from distinct robot conﬁgurations (deﬁned by navigation
speed, manipulation range, etc.). This benchmark comprises 10 dis-
tinct multi-room layouts (Fig. 7a) and 720 task scenarios, providing a
basis for evaluating generalizability across varying spatial structures.
Baselines. To rigorously benchmark algorithmic effectiveness, we
compare our framework against representative baselines spanning
decision-making and communication strategies. Since a few existing
methods naturally support the dynamic team composition required
for Proactive Collaboration, we selected and adapted representative
strategies from standard heterogeneous robot collaboration:
Regarding planning, we compare against: (i) Random (Baseline 1),
serving as a lower bound where agents select skills without delibera-
tion; (ii) Direct_LLM (Baseline 2)19, representing direct LLM generation
with rigid information exchange; and (iii) EMOS (Baseline 3)40, a recent
centralized framework designed for heterogeneous robot coordina-
tion, which we adapted for decentralized execution. Crucially, for the

To elucidate the mechanisms underlying the observed performance
differences from a collaboration perspective, we conducted a ﬁne-
grained failure analysis. We categorize failures into three distinct
mechanistic levels: (i) Capability Deﬁcit (Structural Failure), where

task allocation); and (iii) Reasoning Error (Intra-Agent Cognitive
Failure), where the dominant failure is attributable to an individual
agent acting in isolation based on ﬂawed LLM logic, independent of
team dynamics (e.g., context loss over long sequences, semantic

The emergence of these sophisticated behaviors offers signiﬁcant

results indicate that decentralized natural language coordination can
support timely role negotiation and dynamic subgroup formation
during embodied task execution. More broadly, these observed
behaviors point to a pathway where local autonomy gives rise to
coherent group-level intelligence. This aligns with theories of collec-
tive intelligence in human teams, where performance is driven by
adaptive interaction patterns and self-organized restructuring29,31.
However, we acknowledge that the identiﬁed taxonomy is likely not
exhaustive. We envision that more systematic observation of long-
term interactions will reveal additional emergent behaviors, repre-
senting a promising direction for multi-robot sociology.
Rationale for the robot pool. The robot pool is grounded in the
necessity of efﬁcient resource management within practical deploy-
ments. Assigning an entire ﬂeet to a single task consumes excessive
resources and is often infeasible due to physical overcrowding and
communication bandwidth limits. The pool, therefore, acts as a phy-
sical buffer of available resources, such as standby agents waiting at
logistics distribution hubs. Conceptually, the pool also represents
broader available system capacity. In warehousing scenarios, specia-
lized units remain in staging areas and function as a reserve until pri-
mary robots explicitly request assistance. Furthermore, even when
robots are engaged in other routine duties, an urgent request can
reassign agents from lower-priority tasks. This dynamic effectively
treats the entire system as a resource pool relative to the active
operation. Consequently, our framework naturally aligns with these
realistic constraints.
Limitations and future work. The present study validates the
Proactive Collaboration paradigm within indoor collaborative scenar-
ios. While our simulations establish statistical robustness, the real-
world experiments demonstrate the feasibility of autonomous role
negotiation using representative heterogeneous teams. We acknowl-
edge that further testing across larger sample sizes is required to prove
statistical robustness in physical settings. Furthermore, deployment in
unstructured or adversarial environments introduces additional com-
plexity regarding communication stability and spatial interference.
Looking forward, we aim to extend the Proactive Collaboration
paradigm to more unstructured and constrained environments.
Domains such as warehouse automation, disaster search and rescue1,
and subterranean exploration5 represent promising directions where
dynamic team resizing is critical, but communication bandwidth is
limited. Future work will explore how this framework for decentralized
coordination generalizes to larger and more diverse robot ﬂeets. Fur-
thermore, future research will investigate the integration of more
sophisticated empathy-inspired mechanisms to foster ﬂexible and
effective proactivity.

success of an executed low-level action and the resulting state infor-

This module follows a two-stage pipeline that (i) deterministically
determines whether an executed primitive action succeeds and pro-

After each low-level action, stage (i) performs a rule-based out-
come check. It compares the pre-action and post-action states and
evaluates simple geometric cues, such as relevant distances. It outputs
a success ﬂag. If the action fails, it additionally provides a coarse and
veriﬁable failure reason.
In stage (ii), we provide the LLM with the structured outcome
from stage (i) along with compact pre-action and post-action state
summaries. Conditioned on these grounded signals, the LLM identiﬁes
the speciﬁc cause of failure and generates a concrete recovery strat-

module or directly initiates communication. Based on this diagnosis,
the robot decides whether teammate coordination is necessary. If
coordination is required, it initiates a new round of team commu-
nication and integrates the reﬂection into its Purposeful Expression.
Otherwise, it sends the recovery plan directly to the action decision
module to regenerate a feasible plan.

the real world, failure diagnosis is based on rich, hardware-level feed-

torque sensor readings for slippage, and navigation failures are
assessed using fused LiDAR and IMU data. In simulation, assessment
relies on logical checks against the simulator’s ground-truth state. A
grasp failure is determined by checking kinematic reachability, and
navigation failures are identiﬁed by comparing the ﬁnal position to the
target coordinates. This dual approach ensures that our reasoning
module receives physically meaningful feedback in the real world and
logically consistent feedback in simulation.

Autonomous need-driven communication
While Purposeful Expression determines what a robot should say and
generates a single targeted utterance, Autonomous Need-Driven
Communication orchestrates the entire communication process.
When a robot detects a coordination need and initiates communica-
tion, this mechanism manages the subsequent multi-round dialog until
an actionable consensus is reached. In doing so, it provides the coor-
dination backbone that transforms individual, purpose-driven utter-
ances into team-level agreements: it bridges individual robots and
global coordination by structuring multi-round interactions in which
task allocation, coordination plans, and recruitment decisions are
jointly produced through thorough discussion.
We model the multi-round dialog as a breadth-ﬁrst traversal (BFS)
over a dynamically evolving communication graph G = (V, E), where
vertices V are the participating robots and edges E represent directed
messages. The process, detailed in Algorithm 1, begins with a set of
seed speakers(the robots that initiate communication) Vseed ⊆V. In
each round, a current speaker v ∈V generates an utterance and
explicitly names a set of target robots Vtarget. These robots are added to
the graph, and an edge is created from v to each v0 2 V target. The
protocol schedules these new robots to speak in subsequent rounds,
thereby expanding the graph on demand. The dialog terminates
naturally when no new robots are addressed, signifying that a con-
sensus or saturation point has been reached.
To ensure efﬁciency and robustness, the protocol incorporates
several lightweight pruning and safety mechanisms, including a turn
limit on pairwise conversations to avoid deadlocks. This graph-based
approach provides a ﬂexible yet structured mechanism for decen-
tralized team formation and task allocation, allowing complex coor-
dination plans to be negotiated without a central controller.
